title: Customer Characteristics in Market Research
context: Consider a household detergent producer that promotes one standard formula nationwide without tailoring messages to regional income differences. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Market segmentation divides a market into relatively homogeneous subgroups of customers who share relevant characteristics.
Geographic segmentation groups customers according to where they live or operate, such as a city and its surrounding area.
Demographic segmentation uses measurable social characteristics such as age, gender, education level, and income level.
Psychographic segmentation reflects attitudes, values, lifestyle interests, and willingness to pay for particular product philosophies.
Market segmentation requires every customer in a subgroup to be identical in all personal characteristics.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Segmentation creates subgroups that are relatively homogeneous with respect to relevant customer characteristics.
TRUE — Location-based grouping such as city and surrounding area is geographic segmentation.
TRUE — Age, gender, education, and income are textbook demographic segmentation variables.
TRUE — Attitudes, values, and lifestyle interests underpin psychographic segmentation.
FALSE — Segmentation creates relatively homogeneous subgroups, not perfectly identical individuals.

title: Geographic Segmentation by Location
context: Analyze geographic segmentation based on location such as city and surrounding area. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Geographic segmentation classifies customers by income level and education rather than by location.
Demographic segmentation is defined by lifestyle attitudes and values rather than age or income.
Psychographic segmentation is defined solely by postal district and city boundaries.
Behavioural segmentation ignores how customers buy or use products and focuses only on gender.
Behavioural segmentation distinguishes customers by how they buy or use products, such as occasional versus heavy use.
tactical_explanations: FALSE — Income and education are demographic variables; geographic segmentation uses location.
FALSE — Attitudes and values belong to psychographic segmentation; demographics use age, income, and similar traits.
FALSE — Location defines geographic segmentation, not psychographic segmentation.
FALSE — Behavioural segmentation uses buying and usage patterns; gender is demographic.
TRUE — Buying and usage patterns such as occasional versus heavy use define behavioural segmentation.

title: Demographic Segmentation Variables
context: Review demographic segmentation using age, gender, education level, and income level. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A useful segment should be measurable so that its size and purchasing power can be estimated.
A useful segment should be profitable so that serving it is worthwhile for the business.
A useful segment should be accessible through communication channels and distribution channels that can reach it.
A segment is measurable only when every member has been individually interviewed.
A segment is profitable whenever it is large, even if serving it costs more than the revenue gained.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Measurability requires that segment size and purchasing power can be estimated.
TRUE — Profitability means the segment must be worth serving commercially.
TRUE — Accessibility requires reachable communication and distribution channels.
FALSE — Measurability requires estimable size and purchasing power, not interviewing every member.
FALSE — Profitability requires worthwhile returns; size alone does not guarantee profit.

title: Psychographic Segmentation and Values
context: Analyze psychographic segmentation reflecting attitudes, values, and lifestyle interests. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A useful segment should be durable in the sense that it does not change too quickly to support planning.
A segment is accessible if it is profitable, regardless of whether communication or distribution can reach it.
Targeting is the process of evaluating each segment's attractiveness and selecting one or more segments to enter.
A target market is a group of people or businesses toward whom a firm markets goods, services, or ideas with a strategy designed for their specific needs and preferences.
Positioning is the process by which marketers try to create an image or identity in the minds of their target market.
tactical_explanations: TRUE — Durability means the segment should remain stable enough for planning rather than vanishing immediately.
FALSE — Accessibility is separate from profitability and requires reachable channels.
TRUE — Targeting evaluates attractiveness and chooses segment(s) to enter.
TRUE — The target market receives a tailored strategy aimed at its specific needs and preferences.
TRUE — Positioning builds an image or identity in the target market's minds.

title: Behavioural Segmentation Patterns

statements: A durable segment must never change over time in order to qualify for targeting.
After segments are identified and a target market is chosen, positioning clarifies which product meets the demands of the targeted subgroup.
Targeting means dividing the market into subgroups, while segmentation means choosing which subgroup to enter.
Mass marketing ignores different market segments and offers the same product to all customers.
Positioning occurs before segmentation and targeting in the marketing strategy sequence.
tactical_explanations: FALSE — Durability means not changing too quickly, not permanent immutability.
TRUE — Positioning links the chosen target subgroup to the product that meets its demands.
FALSE — Segmentation divides the market; targeting selects segment(s) to enter.
TRUE — Mass marketing treats the market as undifferentiated with one product for all.
FALSE — Segmentation and targeting precede positioning in the STP sequence.

TRUE — Universal staples like pens, soaps, and detergents commonly suit mass marketing.
FALSE — Mass marketing offers the same product broadly; tailored segment products are segment marketing.

FALSE — Buyers in an Austrian city and its surrounding commuter area illustrate geographic, not psychographic segmentation.
FALSE — Buyers unwilling to pay the full price of a brand-new device reflect psychographic, not purely behavioural segmentation.
